clue.text: This chap will mess up father role extremely fast

parts.note: this chap is he, so 'this chap will' contracts to he'll

indicators.note: to mess something up is to jumble it, so the letters of 'father role' are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man warns he will make a mess of the paternal role, very quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This chap will' gives HE'LL, the apostrophe ignored. 'mess up' rearranges the letters of 'father role'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means at breakneck speed, as a rider tearing along with saddle leather straining.

clue.text: Wait a moment as stud may do

explanation.surface: A plea for patience, likened to what happens on a horse-breeding farm.
explanation.walkthrough: A stud here is a farm keeping horses for breeding, so it literally keeps hold of its animals.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a call to slow down and be patient; a stud farm, which keeps stallions, literally retains its stock.

clue.text: Bishop's following — over one million

indicators.note: one piece lying over another, enclosing it, signals a container here

parts.note: something following comes later
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A bishop's congregation is said to number more than a million.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' puts I (one) and M (million) inside LATER (following). The 's after Bishop is read as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Latimer was a Tudor Bishop of Worcester, burnt at Oxford as a Protestant martyr.

clue.text: Changing sides for skin's getting raw

indicators.note: the sides are left and right, so swapping sides turns the letter L into R

parts.note: skin and flesh both stand for the body's surface, as in flesh-coloured

explanation.surface: Switching from one side to the other leaves someone's skin sore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing sides' swaps L (left) for R (right) in FLESH (skin).
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone new and inexperienced, as a raw or green recruit is.

clue.text: Tougher soldiers given a lift on destroyer

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting a word turns it upwards, so it is read backwards

parts.note: OR stands for other ranks, ordinary soldiers
a buster is something that destroys, as in crime-buster

explanation.surface: Hardier troops are winched aboard a warship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given a lift' turns the soldiers upwards in this down entry. The warship sense of 'destroyer' is the trap; a buster is anything that destroys.
explanation.definitionFit: Robust means strong and sturdy, so its comparative form describes something hardier.

clue.text: Like medal picked up for alcoholic drink

parts.note: eg, for example, introduces something like what was mentioned

indicators.note: in a down clue picking a word up turns it upwards so it reads backwards

parts.note: a gong is British slang for a medal or award

explanation.surface: Someone picks up something resembling a medal, swapping it for a strong drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' looks like a homophone signal, but in a down entry it turns the medal upwards. Gong is British slang for a medal.
explanation.definitionFit: This creamy drink of beaten egg, milk and spirits such as rum or brandy is a Christmas favourite.

clue.text: Somebody following score in card game

indicators.note: one piece following another sits after it, here below it in the down entry

parts.note: a score is twenty
somebody can be called one, as in 'one never knows'

explanation.surface: A person comes after a tally of points in a game of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the casino card game also called blackjack or pontoon, aiming for a hand totalling that number.

clue.text: Give the right name …

explanation.surface: Read with the next clue, it seems to ask for the correct name of a creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this clue to the next, but each is solved separately.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a person a claim to something, or to give a book its title, are both senses of the verb.

clue.text: … Of predator disturbed with one's prod?

definitions.text: Of predator disturbed with one's prod?

indicators.note: disturbed means thrown into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: one is I and 's is is, giving the letters I S

explanation.surface: Following on from the previous clue, it asks the name of a hunter roused by a poke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbed' scrambles the three pieces, one's read as 'one is'. The whole clue also describes the creature: poke its hinged burrow lid and the hunter inside reacts.
explanation.definitionFit: This burrowing arachnid hides under a hinged lid of silk and soil and springs out on passing prey.

clue.text: Refuse to give such a person bad character?

definitions.text: Refuse to give such a person bad character?

parts.words: Refuse to give such a person bad character?
parts.note: read refuse as rubbish: someone who drops rubbish earns a poor name, and bug is a slangy word for a pest

explanation.surface: Someone declines to write an unfavourable reference for a person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as the verb decline, but it is the noun meaning rubbish, which this person drops.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the American word for someone who carelessly drops rubbish in public places.

clue.text: Timepiece salesman left in diner

indicators.note: the salesman has left, so his letters are taken out of the timepiece

parts.note: a repeater is a watch that strikes the hours again when a button is pressed
rep, short for representative, is a travelling salesman

explanation.surface: A watch salesman has been left sitting in a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' removes REP (salesman) from the front of REPEATER (a chiming watch).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone dining is a person who eats.

clue.text: It's a state old politician gets into

indicators.note: one piece getting into another goes inside it

parts.note: OH is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Ohio
MP, Member of Parliament, is a British politician

explanation.surface: A former politician enters some condition, which is said to be the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets into' sets the old politician inside the state. 'It' here is slang for sex appeal, as in the It Girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang for vitality or sex appeal, the quality a star has.

clue.text: Baseball player rejects dope after strong drinks

indicators.note: one piece after another is placed following it

parts.note: shorts are small measures of spirits

indicators.note: to reject is to throw back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: pot and dope are both slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: A ballplayer turns down drugs after a session on the spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejects' reads dope's synonym backwards, making TOP. A short is a measure of spirits, the usual British pub sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A baseball fielder positioned between second and third base has this name.

clue.text: Drunk leaves before time, crossing garden unevenly

indicators.note: one piece crossing another lies across it, so it sits inside

parts.note: early means before the expected time

indicators.note: the uneven, odd-numbered letters of garden are taken

explanation.surface: An inebriated person departs ahead of schedule, lurching across a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' reads as a drunkard but is a past participle: leaves that are drunk. 'unevenly' picks garden's odd letters and 'crossing' sets them inside the time word.
explanation.definitionFit: This blend of black tea flavoured with bergamot is brewed from leaves that people drink.

clue.text: Woodchuck in corner, covered by earth

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece covered by another sits beneath it

parts.note: ground and earth are both words for soil
to corner a market is to hog it, keeping it all for oneself

explanation.surface: A small burrowing animal is trapped in a corner and buried under soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covered by' puts HOG (corner, as in monopolise) under GROUND (earth). 'corner' is a verb, not a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Both names refer to the same North American marmot.

clue.text: Steps taken when cricketer, losing wicket, gets duck

indicators.note: the cricketer loses a letter, which is taken out

parts.note: a bowler delivers the ball in cricket
W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wicket
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A bowler takes a wicket and then is out for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' removes W (wicket) from BOWLER, then O (duck, a zero score) follows. Cricket is the bat-and-ball game, and a bowler there is the one delivering the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: The bolero is a Spanish dance, and steps can mean a dance.

clue.text: Post-war new town's safe, sheltered area

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
the lee is the side sheltered from the wind

explanation.surface: A town built after the war is described as secure and protected.
explanation.walkthrough: PETERLEE is a new town in County Durham, northern England, built from 1948. The 's after town is read as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: This settlement was one of the British new towns built after the Second World War.

clue.text: Criminal with unlimited good or bad luck

parts.note: hood, short for hoodlum, is a gangster

indicators.note: without its limits, the first and last letters, only the middle of good is used

explanation.surface: A crook whose fortune is endlessly either good or bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlimited' strips good of its first and last letters, leaving OO. Hoodoo is chiefly American, a jinx.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a jinx or curse, something that brings misfortune.

clue.text: Affectionate term for female vet in us? Extremely respectful

parts.note: a veteran is an old hand, and GI is an American soldier

indicators.note: the extremes of respectful are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A fond nickname for a woman who treats animals, here in America, said very respectfully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vet in us' reads US as the USA: an old soldier there is an OLD GI. 'Extremely' adds RL, the first and last letters of respectful.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a fond way to address a woman or wife, and also names a school's former pupil.

clue.text: Setter thoroughly overwhelmed by ridicule?

indicators.note: one piece overwhelmed by another is swallowed inside it

parts.note: to jeer is to mock or ridicule
well means thoroughly, as in shake well

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler is completely flattened by mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overwhelmed by' sets the adverb inside the mockery. 'Setter' looks like the crossword compiler but means someone who sets gems.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who mounts precious stones in rings and brooches sets them.

clue.text: Intellectual made to support labour leader

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece supporting another sits under it
the leader of labour is its first letter

parts.note: to have made money is to have earned it

explanation.surface: A thinker was brought in to back the leader of the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' gives L, the first letter of labour, and 'to support' sets EARNED (made) beneath it. Labour is a British political party, but here it is just a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe someone scholarly and well read.

clue.text: Council's struggle in case of awful boozer

indicators.note: one piece in the case of another is enclosed by it

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunkard
to vie is to compete or struggle

explanation.surface: A committee is fighting over a terrible drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in case of' sets the struggle inside the boozer; 'awful' only colours the boozer. The 's after Council is read as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Russian the word means an elected workers' assembly, the basis of the old USSR.

clue.text: Tailor ignored note, making woman's coat

indicators.note: to tailor something is to cut and reshape it, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A dressmaker overlooked a message while making a lady's jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailor' rearranges IGNORED with TE (note). 'Tailor' looks like a noun, the dressmaker, but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: This long, fitted coat for women derives from the riding coat, its name borrowed via French.

clue.text: Top dog's bite

explanation.surface: The pack leader's bite.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the verb meaning to chew noisily, as a horse champs at the bit.
explanation.definitionFit: Top dog is informal for a winner, the short form of champion; to bite is to chomp or munch.

clue.text: Groom with love for jazz band

parts.note: to groom hair is to comb it
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A bridegroom and his beloved hire musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' reads as the bridegroom but is the verb for tidying hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A small jazz group is informally called this, short for combination.

clue.text: Eg Cavell dressed it, having bandages

indicators.note: the words wrap around the answer like a bandage, so it lies inside them

explanation.surface: The famous nurse treated a wound by applying dressings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bandages' signals that the name is hidden across 'dressed it, having'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cavell was a British nurse shot in 1915 for helping Allied soldiers escape occupied Belgium.

clue.text: Spinning old lie about blokes being star-crossed

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go about another piece, surrounding it
spinning a tale twists it, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: blokes is informal British for men

explanation.surface: Telling an ancient lie about men proves to be unlucky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spinning' rearranges OLDLIE to ILLOED, which goes 'about' MEN (blokes).
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean doomed by fate, as Romeo and Juliet were.

clue.text: One revealing cause of crash given fine (not heavy) by judge

parts.note: F is an abbreviation for fine, as on pencils
light means not heavy
a recorder is a part-time judge in the courts of England and Wales

explanation.surface: Someone explains a crash after a fine is handed out by the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: A RECORDER is a barrister who sits as a part-time judge in England and Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The black box on an aircraft logs data that investigators use to find why it came down.
